†*142.  SHRI MOTILAL VORA:††

(a) whether Government are considering grant of permission for opening

(d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement

jurisdiction of the State/UT Governments. There is no system of 
permission/registration/recognition of such private placement agencies by the 
Government, excepting for private manpower exporting employment agencies 
which come under the Emigration Act, 1983 and labour contractors who come 
under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and Inter-State

Statement 
(a) to (c) All the major Central Trade Unions (non-BMS) observed a 
nation-wide Satyagraha on January 8, 2003. Their demands were: 
(i) halt to privatisation of profit making and potentially viable public 
sector undertakings; 
(ii) no changes in the labour laws, including the Industrial Disputes 
Act and the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 
favouring the employers and against the interest of workers; 
(iii) restoration of quantitative restrictions on imports, the removal of 
which is much to the detriment of industry, agriculture and 
national interest as a whole; 
(iv) no to policies leading to serve aggravation of joblessness and 
unemployment and evolving nation-wide employment generation 
policies and programme; 
    (v) well   thought-out   social   security   schemes   including 
unemployment insurance scheme; 
(vi) immediate enactment of compre hensive legislation for agriculture 
workers; 
(vii) amendment of Payment of Bonus Act by removing all ceilings; and 
(viii) restoration of 12 per cent interest on E.P.F. deposits. 
The Ministry of Labour is conscious of the concern of the Central Trade 
Union. Various amendments in the labour laws are considered with a view to 
promoting harmonious industrial relations after adequate consultation with all 
the social partners. The requirements of growing and competitive economy 
will, however, be kept in view while proposing changes in the labour laws.

(a) whether a high level inter-ministerial meeting was held by the Prime 
Minister to find a solution to the current crisis in sugar industry; and 
(b) if so, the details of the discussion which took place and the 
steps being taken to end the crisis? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Discussions have taken place in recent weeks, including in the 
context of a representation of the Maharashtra Rajya Sahakari Sakhar 
Karkhana Sangh, to address the difficulties encountered in the sugar industry 
following a general fall in prices. 
2. The steps initiated to assist the industry include the creation of a Buffer 
Stock of 20 lakh tonnes for a period of one year involving an outgo of Rs. 412 
crores from the Sugar Development Fund, in addition to which about Rs. 374 
crores are expected to be released by banks on account of the Buffer Stock. 
Thus, about Rs. 786 crores would become available to the sugar industry for the 
payment of cane price dues to the farmers. The factory-wise allocation of the 
Buffer Stock (provisional) has been made and communicated to the sugar 
factories in January, 2003. 
3. In order to further promote exports of sugar (to liquidate surplus 
stocks), it has been decided that neutralization of ocean freight disadvantage 
at the rate of Rs. 350 per tonne on export shipments of sugar would be 
reimbursed to sugar factories with effect from 14th February, 2003.

(a) whether cane growers have been agitating over recovery of arrears of their 
dues amounting to Rs. 11,000 crore from the sugar mills; 
(b) if so, the details of the memorand a or representations received from 
the canegrowers during the past three months; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to ensure payment of their dues? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
There have been sporadic incidents of agitation by sugarcane growers in 
respect of payment of cane price due/cane price being offered by the sugar 
mills. Representations in this behalf have, inter-alia, been received from the 
Swantantra Bharat Paksh, Maharashtra and the Kissan Sangh, B udhana 
(Muzaffarnagar). The cane price dues for the last season 2001 -2002 (as on 
31.1.2003), as reported by the State authorities, stand at about Rs. 363.65 crores. 
2. The following steps have been taken to facilitate speedy clearance of dues 
of sugarcane growers: 
(i) A Buffer Stock of 20 lakh tonnes of sugar has recently been 
created, as a result of which the sugar factories would receive a 
subsidy amount of Rs. 412 crores (from the Sugar Development 
Fund) for the exclusive purpose of  payment of cane price dues. In 
addition, about Rs. 374 crores would become available from the 
banks on account of additional margin money. Thus, about Rs. 786 
crores would be available to the sugar factories to clear the payments 
of cane price dues to sugarcane growers. 
(ii) The levy obligation of sugar factories has been reduced to 10% w.e.f. 
1st March, 2002 to enable the factories to sell more sugar under 
free-sale quota in the open market. 
(iii) The sugar factories have been extended temporary relief by way of 
permission to sell equivalent quantity of unlifted levy sugar stocks 
as free sale sugar in the open market. During

Development Fund (SDF), Act, 1982 and the SDF Rules, 1983           
have been amended to neutralise the internal transport and  ocean 
freight disadvantage.

Disinvestment of PSUs 
*141.    SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned 'Politics stalled NALCO sale' which appeared in the 'Hindustan Times', 
dated the 2nd November, 2002; 
(b) whether disinvestment process of NALC0, EIL, RCF, Neyvelli 
Lignite Corporation Limited and BEML are being delayed, deliberately; and 
(c) if not, the reasons for not moving fast on the disinvestment of the above 
PSUs? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY AND MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN 
SHOURIE):(a)Yes,Sir. 
(b) There is no proposal for disinvestment of Bharat Earth Movers Ltd. 
(BEML). Government has not yet decided about disinvestment in Neyveli 
Lignite Company Ltd. (NLC). Government has decided to defer the 
consideration of proposal of disinvestment in Rashtriya Chemicals and 
Fertilisers Ltd. (RCF). Disinvestment in Engineers India Ltd. (EIL) and 
National Aluminium Company Ltd. (NALCO) are at different stages of 
process. In the case of NALCO, the plant visit by the Qualified Interested Parties 
(QIPs) was suspended due to agitation with effect from 29th October, 2002. 
36 

[27 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) Government implements the disinvestment programme in a manner 
which is conducive with market conditions and the prevailing ec onomic 
environment. It follows a well defined procedure which involves extensive inter-
ministerial consultation and decision making. Moreover, Government does not 
sell its equity holding in distress and adopts a graduated approach towards 
disinvestment. While sometime causing delays this approach ensures that the 
sales realisation is maximized and the transfer of management control to the 
strategic partner is successfully completed. 
Poor telecom network 
*151. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOW DA: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that telecom ne twork in the country is very poor 
and inadequate for providing phones to rural areas in the country and if so, 
the reasons therefor; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the growth during the recent years has 
been concerntrated in urban areas; if so, the details of the teledensity in urban and 
rural population during the last three years; 
(c) whether Karnataka figures poorly in terms of providing access to 
phones in rural areas; and 
(d) if so, the steps proposed to be taken to improve phone services in rural 
areas of the State? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY AND DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) No, 
Sir. It is not a fact that the Telecom Network in the country is poor. However, 
the progress has been slow in rural areas due to inadequate availability of 
funds, equipments and materials alongwith fast changing technolgoies. 
Irregular or absence of power supply, insufficient accessibility and scattered 
demand have also contributed to slow and tardy growth of Telecom Network 
in these areas. Further the Telecom Services in rural areas have been 
unattractive due to low revenue and high cost per DEL (Direct Exchange 
Lines); 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2003] 
(b) The growht of DELs in an area is dependent upon demand which in turn 
depends upon economy, literacy rate, commercial actlvites and per capita 
income etc. Growth of telecom has been obsered in both urban as well as rural 
areas in the last few years. However, the rate of growth in urban areas in more as 
compared to the rural areas. The teledensity per hundred population in urban 
and rural areas of the last three years is given as under:  
Year Rural Urban 
1999-2000 0.68 7.64 
2000-2001 0.93 10.16 
2001-2002 1.21 12.22 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Improvement in telecom services is a continuous process. 
Following steps are taken in phased manner in the country including rural 
areas of Karnataka: 
(i) Majority of connections are planned to be given through Wireless 
in Local Loop (WLL) network for which equipment is likely to be 
received during 2003-04. 
(ii) Fault repair services are comput erized and centralized at all short 
distance charging centres for round the clock booking of faults 
and their prompt rectification. 
(iii) Upgradation of external plant. 
(iv) Replacement of old paper core cables by jelly filled cables. 
(v) Replacement of life expired telephone instruments.

*156. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some new methods have been adopted to measure 
poverty and calculate the number of people Below Poverty Line; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that a numb er of States have raised several 
questions in this regard; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and Government's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) No, Sir.The present method used by the 
Planning Commission for estimation of poverty is based on the methodology 
recommended by the Expert Group on 'Estimation of Proportion and Number 
of Poor' (Lakdawala Committee). The Expert Group, which was constituted in 
September, 1989 submitted its Report to the Planning Commission in July, 
1993. A full Planning Commission meeting chaired by the Prime Minister in 
March, 1997 accepted the recommendations of the Expert Group with minor 
modifications. Since then the estimates of poverty at National and State level 
are being made using the Expert Group methodology. 
(b) In view of (a) above, does not arise. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The Planning Commission has received representation 
from the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Orissa in 
the matter of choice of the methodology of estimation of poverty. The State 
Governments of Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka urged that in estimating 
poverty the impact of the price depr essing effect of the food subsidy 
scheme, funded from the State Exche quer, be eliminated. The Government 
of Andhra Pradesh at a later stage urged that estimates should be made 
on the basis of earlier methodology of poverty estimation, known as the 
Task Force method. The Government of Orissa had urged that the national 
level poverty line be adopted for estimating poverty in the State. 
After carefully considering the representations, the Planning 
Commission decided to continue with the Expert Group methodology

sponsored food subsidy scheme, the Planning Commission has raised the

Settlement of consumers disputes 
957. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR RE DDY: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, which was 
enacted to settle the consumers disputes expeditiously, has failed in its basic 
objective; 
(b) if so, whether Government have made any efforts to identify the 
reasons therefor; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) to (d) No, Sir. It is evident from the fact that out of 18,89,538 cases 
filed before the consumer disputes redressal agencies, set up under the 
Consumer Protection Act, 1986,15,48,050 cases (81.9%) have already been 
disposed of by them, which is a considerable achievement by any standard. 
However, the delay in disposal of cases by the consumer disputes 
redressal agencies in the country is a cause of concern. The main contributing 
factors leading to delay are inadequate infrastructure, frequent adjournments, non-
filling up of the posts of the Presidents/Members in the consumer disputes 
redressal agencies etc. To remove these obstacles, some of the important steps 
taken for the speedy disposal of cases by these agencies are as under:— 
(i) One-Time-Grant of Rs. 61.80 crores provided to the States/ UTs by 
the Central Government to supplement their efforts to strengthen the 
infrastructure of the consumer disputes redressal agencies; 
112 

[27 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(ii) Monitoring of the working of consumer disputes redressal 
agencies through the National Commission; 
(iii) States and Union Territories requested to take prompt steps to fill 
up vacant posts of President/Member in the consumer disputes 
redressal agencies and maintain a panel of suitable candidates for 
immediate appointment as President/ Member; 
(iv) The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 has recently been amended in 2002 
mainly to facilitate the quicker disposal of complaints by enhancing 
the capabilities of the consumer forums, strengthening them with 
more powers, streamlining the procedures and widening the scope 
of the Act. Among various important amendments made to facilitate 
quicker disposal of cases include the procedures for selection of the 
Members of the State Commission and President and Members of 
the District Forum have been amended for uninterrupted selection of 
the Members of the State Commission and President and Members 
of the District Forums so as to  fill i'p vacant post of the State 
Commission and the District Forums in time. A provision has also 
been incorporated in the amendment to empower the senior most 
Member to perform as President in the absence of the regular 
President of the National Commission, State Commission and the 
District Forum for smooth and uninterrupted functioning of these 
forums.

959. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether lack of supervision affects PDS badly; and 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2003] 
(b) if so, the steps proposed for vi gilance mechanism against continued 
malpractices by the dealers of fair price shops? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SUBHASH 
MAHARIA): (a) and (b) The Public Distribution System (Control) Order 2001 
provides for stringent punishment under Section 7 of the Essential Commodities 
Act, 1955 against fair price shop owners for malpractices. The Order provides 
the procedure for monitoring of the Public Distribution System including the 
functioning of the Fair Price Shops by the State Governments as under: 
(i) State Governments shall ensure a proper system of monitoring of fair 
price shops and prescribe model sale register, stock register and ration 
card register. 
(ii) State Governments shall ensure regular inspections of fair price shops 
not less than once in six months by the designated authority. State 
Governments may issue orders specifying the inspection schedule, 
list of check points and the authority responsible for ensuring 
compliance with the said orders. 
(Hi) Meetings of the Vigilance Committees on the Public Distribution 
System at the State, District, Block and FPS level shall be held on a 
regular basis. The date and periodicity shall be notified by the State 
Government. However, the periodicity shall not be less than one 
meeting a quarter at all levels.

963. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Government of Rajasthan had brought to the 
notice of the Central Government of the poor quality of foodgrains supplied to it 
during the drought last year; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, Government's reaction to the statement made to the media by the 
Rajasthan officials; and 
(d) what steps were taken by Government to ensure that the goodgrains 
supplied to the drought affected State are of good quality? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
ARRAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SUBHASH 
MAHARIA): (a) to (d) Good quality foodgrains conforming to PFA standards and 
three from insect infestation are issued to State Governments/UT 
Administrations for distribution under Targeted Public Distribution System 
(TPDS) and other welfare schemes. Ample opportunities are provided to the 
officials of the State Governments/UT Administrations to inspect the -stock prior 
to lifting from FCI godowns. Therefore, there are minimal chances of supply of poor 
quality of goodgrains. A few State Governments including Rajasthan had shown 
their reluctance for the supply of lustre lost wheat under TPDS. Lustre lost 
wheat is at par with sound wheat, so far as nutritional value is concerned. 
Keeping in view the reluctance of State Governments towards lustre lost wheat, 
its supply was stopped to State Governments from 6th August, 2002. 
The following additional steps have been taken by the Government to 
ensure that the foodgrains supplied to the States including drought-affected 
States are of good quality:— 
(i) Instructions have been issued to all the State Governments/ UT 
Administrations that an officer not below the rank of Inspector should 
be deputed to check the quality of foodgrains before their lifting 
from the FCI godowns. 
(ii) The samples of goodgrains are jointly drawn and sealed by the officers 
of the State Governments/UT Administrations and the FCI during 
the issue of stocks from FCI godowns for display at the counters of 
Fair Price Shops (FPSs). 
120 

[27 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(iii) The officers of the State Governments' and the Ministry c onducted 
surprise checks of the FPSs to ove r see the quality of foodgrains 
being distributed through TPDS. 
(iv) The officers of the Department designated as 'Area Officers' for 
monitoring the TPDS work in the respective States also undertake 
visits to the storage depots and the FPSs, during their visit to the 
States to check the quality of foodgrains being issued.

Pesticides in bottled water 
968. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJ ARY: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item titled 
'Pesticides in bottled water' appearing in  the 'Times of India', dated the 5th 
February, 2003; 
(b) if so, what are the details in this regard togetherwith the number of the 
licensees and quantity of bottles produced and consumed in India; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2003] 
(c)-whether it is a fact that the testing norms prescribed by BIS are not of 
international standards; 
(d) whether Government propose to suspend the bottling activity until 
suitable testing norms is adopted by BIS considering the adverse impact on 
health of the consumers; and 
(e) if not, the reasons thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) to (e) Two Indian Standards, one for Natural Mineral Water and 
another for Packaged Drinking Water, were formulated in 1998. These 
standards cover microbiological, physical and chemical safety of water. These 
standards were based on international standards prevailing at that time. In March 
2001, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare enforced a gazetted notification 
under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules 1955 as per which Packaged 
Drinking Water and Mineral Water cannot be manufactured, sold or exhibited for 
sale without BIS Standards Mark th ereby making BIS Certification Mark 
Mandatory. Ministry of Health is the enforcement authority and BIS is the 
certifying agency. BIS has so far granted more than 700 licences for packaged 
drinking water (Including 1 in Nepal) and 6 licences for packaged natural mineral 
water (including one in France) to different manufacturers. The water 
manufactured in adherence to these standards is entirely fit for human 
consumption. According to the existing BIS Standard pesticide residues 
should be below detectable limits when tested by the relevant method specified 
in the Indian Standards. This is in  accordance with th e Prevention of Food 
Adulteration Rules, 1955. A seminar was covened by BIS on 13th February, 
2003 to determine whether the existing product was fit for human consumption, 
The seminar was attended by eminent Scientists representing Government 
bodies, representative of World Health Organisation, Consumers, 
representatives of Industry and other stakeholders. The seminar affirmed that 
the Packaged Drinking Water now be ing produced accord ing to the BIS 
Standards is fit for human consumption. In view of these facts, the question of 
suspending bottling activity does not arise.

Target of Disinvestment 
986. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI  : Will the Minister of 
DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the target set for disinvestment during 2002-2003; 
(b) how far the target has been achieved; and 
(c) the reasons for shortfall in achieving the target? 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) 
The target for the amount to be realised through disinvestment in PSUs during 
2002-2003 is Rs. 12,000 crore. 
(b) An amount of Rs. 3,342.06 crore has been realised till 26-2-2003 
through disinvestment in PSUs. 
(c) Implementation of the disinvestment programme depends on a variety 
of factors including market cond itions, industry-wise business cycle 
fluctuations, interest of the prospective bidders, the adequacy of the price bid 
etc. Moreover, Government does not sell its equity holding in distress. In cases 
where the value of land and buildings is significant, often the delay occurs 
because the property rights are unclear and legally establishing these property 
rights takes time, though it is necessary to do so to maximise the realisable 
value. In view of this it is not always possible to meet the annual targets. 
Re-evaluation of Disinvestment Procedure 
987. SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: Will the Minister of 
DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government think that the disinvestment procedure deviated 
itself from the declared objectives; 
148 

[27 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) whether any case of under valuation of profit making PSU has been brought 
in to the notice of Government at the time of disinvestment process; 
(c) whether it is a fact that disinvestment replaces PSU monopoly by private 
monopoly; 
(d) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(e) Government's opinion to use the disinvestment procedures in education, 
health, employment and small scale sectors; and 
(f) whether Government consider to re-evaluate the procedures of 
disinvestment? 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) No, 
Sir. 
(b) Articles have appeared in newspapers alleging undervaluation of shares of 
some of the PSUs disinvested. Government does not agree with the views 
expressed in these articles. For valuation several assumptions are made to value 
assets, liabilities and future business prospects of the company being disinvested. It 
is used to arrive at a reserve price. The actual sale price is determined through a 
process of competitive bidding, which allows the market determined valuation, at the 
point in time, to be revealed,including the control premium, realisable from the bidders, 
for transfer of management control in the case of strategic sale. Subsequent changes 
in the market price of shares of disinvested PSUs reflect, among other things, future 
prospects of the company under the new management. 
(c) and (d) There is no evidence so far that the disinvestment has resulted in 
abuse of market dominance. The abuse of private monopoly in an industrial sector 
can always be checked by the Government through appropriate regulation and 
by allowing competition from imports. 
(e) The mandate of the Ministry of Disinvestment is for disinvestment 
in Public Sector Undertakings only. 
(f) The procedure for disinvestment has evolved over a period of time 
149 

RAJYA  SABHA [27 February, 2003] 
and is continuously reviewed, updated and refined on the basis of experience 
gained. It has also gone through the process of judicial review in the context of 
several cases relating to disinvestment and in all such cases, the procedure 
followed has been upheld.

Gadgil-Mukherjee Formula 
 
†1046.    SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the Gadgil-Mukherjee Formula; 
(b) whether it is a fact that in  the recent meeting of National 
Development Council some States have stated the formula being promoter 
of non-development; 
(c) if so, Government's reaction thereto; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that the NSSO has indicated the under 
calculation of the population living Below the Poverty Line in various States; 
(e) if so, the steps being taken by Government to provide the correct 
information about the persons living Below the Poverty Line; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) The Gadgil Formula as approved by the 
National Development Council (NDC) in December 1991 is the basis for the 
allocation of Normal Central Assist ance (NCA) for the Annual Plans of 
States. The Formula takes into account their relatives backwardness as well 
as their performance in the fiscal front and in 
achieving national objectives. 
 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
202 

[27 February, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) and (c) There is wide diverg ence in the views among the State 
Government regarding the formula. In general, while the advanced States prefer 
higher weightage in the Formula for performance, the less advanced States have 
sought higher weightage for backward ness. Hence the Full Planning 
Commission in its meeting held on 27th and 29th June, 2001 and discussed 
inter-alia the issue of revision of Gadgil Formula and in view of the 
divergence of the views among the State Governments and the sensitivity of 
this issue, it was decided that it would be necessary to discuss this further and 
evolve a consensus before alternatives are considered by the National 
Development Council (NDC). 
(d) to (f) The Planning Commission follows a uniform methodology for 
estimation of poverty across all the Stat es. The present method used by the 
Planning Commission for estimation of poverty is based on the methodology 
recommended by the Expert Group on 'Estimation of Proportion and Number 
of Poor' (Lakdawala Committee). The Expert Group, which was constituted in 
September 1989 submitted its Report to the Planning Commission in July 
1993. A full Planning Commission meeting chaired by the Prime Minister in 
March, 1997 accepted the recommendations of the ExDert Group with minor 
modifications. Since then the estimates of poverty at national and State level are 
being made using the expert group methodology.

1072. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:  Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that on the demand from the SSI, the RBI has agreed 
to reduce the lending rates to this sector; 
(b) if so, the details of the demand made with regard to interest by various 
associations of the Small Scale Sect or and the action contemplated by 
Government in this regard;

delayed payments and other things relating to Small Scale Industries; and

THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCA LE INDUSTRIES (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) and (b) The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in its meeting of the 
Standing Advisory Committee on flow of Institutional Credit to Small Scale 
Industries (SSIs) sector held on 15th January, 2003 in which some SSI 
Associations were also present, discussed various issues relating to SSI sector 
including reduction in lending rates to SSI sector. As a follow up, the RBI 
has advised the banks to set the interest rate on advances to SSI sector 
keeping in view prevailing general southward movement in interest rates. 
(c) and (d) There already exists inte rest on delayed payments to Small 
Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertakings Act, 1993, as amended in 1998,

Act provides for penal interest to be paid by buyers to suppliers if payment is 
made after due date and such interest paid by buyers shall not be allowed as 
deduction for the purpose of computation of income under Income Tax Act, 
1961. SSI suppliers can also approach the Industry Facilitation Councils (IFCs)

in regard to delay in payments.

Need to include Tulu Language in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution 
SHRI K.B.KRISHNA MURTHY (Karnataka): The coastal region of 
Karnataka has contributed a lot to our nation in terms of culture, history and 
trading. Dakshin Kannada is a district of  Karnataka; and Mangalore is the port 
city. From centuries, this district has contributed its bit for the shipping 
industry. The Dakshin Kannada region is the home of 60 lakh Tulu-speaking 
people. This Special Mention pertains to the Tulu language, which is spoken 
by the people in Dakshin Kannada and Udupi districts. Tulu language is an 
ancient language and belongs to the Dravidian family and has a legacy of rich 
culture and heritage. The language has an ancient script which has not been 
in use for a long time due to the advent of Kannada and English. Great 
linguists have considered Tulu as a highly-developed language with a rich 
vocabulary. It is our fundamental duty to propagate our art and culture to the 
future generations by creating a circumstance that will not lead to its antiquity. 
In the case of Tulu, it is a language which has been developed by centuries of 
usages, folklores and customs and thereafter became a language. 
Considering the fact that preserving the art and culture is a Directive Principle 
of the State Policy, it is incumbent upon the State to place this language in the 
Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, thereby facilitating its development and 
revival. 
I request the Government to take note of my observation and do the 
needful.   Thank you.

Holding of simultaneous elections to Lok Sabha, State Legislative     
Assemblies and local bodies in the country 
DR. ALLADI P.RAJKUMAR (Andhra Pr adesh): Madam, I am grateful 
to you as well as to the hon. Chairman for providing me this opportunity. This 
is one of the important Sp ecial Mentions which I am raising. I would request 
hon. senior Members of the House, and especially Shri Pranab Mukherjee, to 
give attention to this important matte r. Madam, it is unf ortunate that today 
neither the hon. Leader of the House nor hon. Prime Minister is here. I would 
have been happier if they were present here. I would also like to invite the 
attention of media before starting this Special Mention. 
Madam, I propose to the Government to consider for bringing in a 
new legislation to regulate the Indian elections, right from the local body 
Panchayat elections, municipal election s, State Legislature elections to the 
Parliament elections, to be held simultaneously throughout India on a single 
236 

[27 February, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
day, to avoid huge manpower loss an d monetary loss, besides creating a 
healthy atmosphere in politics. At present, India has virtually only three MPs - 
money power, muscle power and mafia power - which are controlling all 
elections and resist every attempt of reforms. It will make the duties of the 
officials of the Election Commission easier, as they are responsible for holding 
elections and keeping the electoral rolls up to date. 
Though it may seem a far-fetched idea, yet, if considered seriously in 
depth, it will be of tremend ous benefit to the country, particularly in the matter 
of causing unnecessary economic burden  on the nation's exchequer, besides 
a lot of time and energy spent on elections  at different levels. Madam, you will 
remember that at the init ial stages, that is, during 1952 and 1957, elections to 
the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies were held simultaneously, but later 
on, with early dissolutions of some State Assemblies, elections were held at 
different dates, and the practice of si multaneous elections to the Lok Sabha 
and the State Vidhan Sabhas was distur bed and staggered. Now, we see, 
elections are being held through out t he year in one or more States. For 
example, last year, elections to the St ate Assemblies of Gujarat, Uttaranchal, 
Uttar Pradesh, etc. were held. During the current year, elections to several 
State Assemblies are being held. This in volves a lot of expenditure, involving 
a huge amount, to the Government as well as political parties. 
Elections are always important because they are the pith and 
substance of democracy. It would be, howe ver, advisable to hold elections to 
the Lok Sabha, the Legislative Assemblies and the local bodies through out 
the country on a single day, or, at the mo st on two or three days. For security 
and execution of this gigantic work, the entire work force of the paramilitary 
forces and the Police force of the Central Government and State Governments 
can be commissioned. This will save a large amount of money for the country, 
which can, in turn, be used for the development work. 
I request the Government to consider this matter in all seriousness 
and initiate action in this regard through discussions at all levels like the 
National Development Council.

Grave threat to Hirakud Dam in Orissa 
DR. M. N. DAS (Orissa): M adam, after Independence, the 
construction of the multi-purpose Hirakud dam, in Orissa, on the River 
Mananadi, which has a catchment area of  83,000 sq. kms. of the reservoir, 
was taken up as new India's one of the largest developmental projects. It took 
ten years to complete. While inaugurati ng it in 1957, the then Prime Minister, 
Jawaharlal Nehru had described it as a Temple of Modern India'. The main 
objectives of the Hirakud dam were irri gation of hundreds of thousands of 
hectares of land, generation of 900 million units of power annually and control 
of floods. Madam, the Hirakud dam's life span had been calculated to be more 
than hundred years.   But, within forty years, the 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2003]  
continuous sedimentation has reduced its water-storage capacity by 27 per 
cent. The average annual silt deposition is 26 million acre feet, which is faster 
than the usual silting that takes place. The main caus e of fast sedimentation, 
according to experts, is rapid deforestation in the catchment area. Beginning 
from its origin in the Amarkantak Hi lls to the reservoir at Hirakud, the 
Mahanadi Valley is ruthlessly subjected to mining activities, smuggling of 
timber and a continuous increase in th e area of cultivation, which led to 
uprooting of lakhs of trees. There are no afforestation programmes to 
compensate the loss of forest wealth, nor are steps taken to stop the 
smuggling of timber. Added to these,  mining wastes are dumped into the 
reservoir. The Remote Sensing Survey shows that the total silt deposited by 
now in gross-storage comes to much more than 2,000 million cubic metres 
and the dam authorities admit that de-s iltation of the reservoir is just 
impossible, because it may cost more than Rs.12,000 crores. It is time the 
Government of India woke up to face th is challenge in order to save the dam 
before it is late.

Importance of palliative care in treatment of cancer 
MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Among the many 
diseases, which severely affect Indians, cancer is one of the deadliest. We 
have more than three million cancer patie nts in the country, and almost eight 
lac patients are added to this number, annua lly. Eighty per cent of the cases 
are detected so late that the disease is no longer curable. The pain, the 
anguish and the agony of these cancer patients are unimaginable. 
Though, in 1991, the Government of India had declared palliative 
care as an essential component of cancer treatment, yet there has hardly 
been any progress. 
This Special Mention comes to request the Government for inclusion 
of pain management and palliative care in the medical curriculum for 
establishing network of Palliative Care  Centres at cancer hospitals, primary 
health centres, and other outreach ce ntres to create awareness among the 
Government, professionals and public that morphine forms the mainstay of 
cancer pain alleviation; and appropriat e changes in health care and narcotics 
regulations and procedures are required to improve drug availability, and to 
facilitate relevant agencies, including NGOs, in procuring, holding and using 
cheap opioid analgesics like morphine for the benefit of terminal cancer 
patients.

Need for upliftment of other Backward Classes in the country 
SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR (Karnataka): Madam, the backward 
classes and other minorities together cons titute 55 per cent of our country's 
population. However, even after more th an 50 years, the c ondition of OBCs 
has not improved. They are still educ ationally, socially, and economically 
backward. Despite the enabling provisions in the Constitution, and the 
implementation of the Mandal Co mmission's recommendations, the 
Reservation Policy is not being implemented in letter and spirit. The OBCs get 
reservation in Government jobs, but fo r promotions there is no reservation. 
Still these reserved posts are lying vacan t. There is a huge backlog of posts 
meant for OBCs in the Central Gove rnment and in the public sector 
undertakings. 
Similarly, budgetary allocations for social welfare sectors meant for 
upliftment of the OBCs are awfully disp roportionate. And no welfare schemes 
for the OBCs have been announced so fa r. Under the Act pertaining to State 
and National Commissions for Backward Classes, revision of list of backward 
classes is mandatory every ten years. It is due for revision in 2004. Meaningful 
revision of such lists calls for door-to-door survey of the OBCs. Only then 
would we be able to know the benef its reaped by the OBCs since the 
formation of the Commissions. 
I, therefore, urge upon the Governm ent to give the OBCs their due 
share and clear the backlog in Government jobs through special recruitment 
drives. It should also extend reservations in educational institutions forthwith.

Restoration and activation of Buckingham Canal 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Madam, covering a 
distance of 650 kilometres, Buckingham Canal, which links Marakkanam in 
Tamil Nadu and Kakinada in Andhra Pradesh, is the largest inland waterway 
in India. Any effort to restore it will constitute a landmark in our country. It has 
almost 6000 kilometres of sea coast and a thousand kilometres of waterways, 
provided by various rivers of our country. In 1882, when it came into being, 
people used to take advantage of this canal. Farmers and traders from Andhra 
Pradesh used it to carry their agricultural produce and commodities to various 
markets in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. The existing stretches of the 
canal, both in Andhra Pradesh and Tam il Nadu, were used till 1960 and 1985 
respectively.   Constructing such a canal  anew 
255 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2003]  
would require a staggering amount of Rs . 13,000 crores. Since the canal is 
already there, its restoration and oper ation would cost much less. Studies 
reveal that transportation of per tonne of goods, in waterways, is twice and 
four times cheaper than transportation through railways and roads 
respectively. Transportation through road, in terms of volume, density and 
intensive use of energy, is becomin g costlier day by day. Hence the 
reactivation of Buckingham canal would be of great help in promoting the 
economic interests of the people and also  in promoting local tourism. It runs 
along the East Coast and provides an important channel for diverting excess 
flood water to areas and ponds which suffer deficiencies of water during lean 
period. I would request the Government of  India to take expeditious measures 
in restoring and revitalizing this canal and declaring it as a national waterway.

PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM (Tamil Na du): Madam, due to acute 
poverty prevailing in our country, young children are being traded for petty 
sums of money. Recently, four childr en, including one girl of Dindugal of 
Madurai district, Tamil Nadu, who were engaged in sweet meat units, were 
rescued from Nellore in Andhra Pradesh.  All the four are in the age group of 
ten and fourteen. 
Due to acute poverty, their parents sold them, through 
intermediaries, for a very small amount. This inhuman act was brought to the 
notice of the Charitable Service Organisation, SOCC, Trust of Madurai. With 
the help of the district authorities, th is Organisation rescued the children. All 
the children were forced to work from 5 o'clock in the morning till late at night.

atrocities are prevailing throughout t he country. These heart-burning incidents 
are taking place due to extreme poverty. Though the Central Government 
keeps a watchful eye across the country, in many cities, including Delhi, young 
boys and girls below the age of twelve years are used for begging after they 
are cruelly deformed into physically handicapped. A Child Welfare 
Commission needs to be constituted to effectively tackle with this problem.

Kelkar Committee recommendations on agricultural income 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): 
Madam, as per the recommendations made by Kelkar, agricultural income 
should be taxed. If this proposal is ac cepted, it will prove to be detrimental to 
the farming community. After the land reforms have been implemented, there 
are no farmers having large landholdings or huge incomes. For the last five 
years, because of severe drought in almost  half of our country, the situation in 
agriculture sector has been grim. Thousands of farmers have committed 
suicides in various parts of the country. As per the WTO Agreement, foreign 
produce is coming into our country at cheaper rates. Moreoever, every input or 
purchase made by the agricultural community is liable to indirect taxes. Excise 
duty and sales tax are levied on every item farmers buy. Bringing agriculture 
sector in the net of income tax means that farmers will be harassed by the 
income-tax officials. It is a well known fact that farmers would get their credit 
from private lenders at a higher rate of interest. The Government must take 
note of such factors, and this  is not the time to think about tax on agricultural 
income. Because of severe drought situation in 14 States of our country, the 
Government should extend concessions to the agricultural sector. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Central Government to drop all the plans 
to levy tax on agricultural income. Thank you, Madam.

The Election Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2003 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI NILOTPAL BASU): Now, we will take 
up for consideration the Election Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2003. Shri Arun 
Jaitley. 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE AND MINISTER OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY) : Sir, I beg to move : 
261 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2003]  
that the Bill further to amend t he Representation of the People Act, 
1951 and the Indian Penal Code, as passed by Lok Sabha, be taken 
into consideration. 
Sir, the object of the amendment has been to enable those working 
for us in the Armed Forces and various categories governed by this Bill, to 
effectively exercise their right to vo te. So far, facilities have been made 
available to a certain section of our el ectorate, which, on account of call of 
duty, either on account of election duty, or  on account of call of national duty, 
in the security arrangements of the country, are unable to be present in their 
constituencies. The option available to t hem in lieu of physical presence at the 
polling booth, is to cast their vote th rough the postal ballot system. Since the 
amendments have taken place to the R epresentation of the People Act, and 
the effective period for campaign has been reduced to 14 days; this has 
become quite ineffective, in terms of exercise of voting right by a postal ballot. I 
use the word "ineffective" because, to the headquarters of the various Armed 
Force organizations from all constituencies all over the country, postal ballots 
are sent. They are then sorted out and sent to the various regions or areas 
where these personnel are posted. From there, the exact position of each of 
the serving officers or Jawans has to be ascertained and the ballot is then sent 
to them, where it is stamped upon by  them, and then sent back to the 
respective Returning Officers; and 14 da ys is obviously inadequate. And 
experience has shown that the figures vary between the Postal Department 
and the Election Commission. The Election Commission felt that the figures 
are barely about ten per cent or so, people who are able to exercise their 
votes. So, when the matter was being debated in the other House, most 
Members of Parliament, who contested Lok Sabha elections, effectively felt 
that not more than 50 to 100 per consti tuency of these ballots are actually 
received back from officers of the secu rity forces itself. There is a strong 
opinion amongst the security forces that some effective 'right to vote' should be 
given to them. Therefore, this whole idea of permitting them to vote by proxy 
vote, the principle in the Bill, is to make it operational. The Election 
Commission will have to frame detailed rules in this matter, as to how it is to be 
exercised. There would be a category of authorized persons, who would be 
authorized relatives, and there could be an assignment in advance or an 
authorization, much before this entire period, where a person who chooses not 
to be present himself because of call of duty, or alternatively, does not want to 
use the postal ballot system, to use proxy voting system, by which 
262 

[27 February. 2003] RAJYA SABHA  
he can ensure that his vote is cast. It is obviously a voluntary relinquishment 
of that right in favour of an authorized relative, and for those who don't want to 
exercise it this way; the other opti ons, which are existing, are already 
available to them. This is, thus, only an enabling provision. 
Sir, there has been a considerable debate over the last few years as 
to the desirability of this. Most people in  the political process have felt, so also 
the security forces, that this right co uld be made more effective. There have 
been, at times, two views as to how to  make it more effe ctive. Within the 
fourteen days' period, it is quite diffi cult to make the postal ballots system 
effective. That is the reason for the co nflicting views, despite that motivation 
from various political groups. One se t of people have effectively argued that 
since this right to franchise is being effectively declined, denied to a large 
number of them, because of these proc edural and logistical problems, we 
must support this alternative system . The other view, which has been argued 
is that in doing so, we are doing away with the principle of secrecy, which is 
also of great importance, as far as th e election system is concerned. Sir, I 
have tried to examine how this has wo rked out in several other systems all 
over the world. There are a large number  of countries, at least, about 12 of 
them, which in one way or the other, have today formulated this system of 
proxy voting for categories of electorate. The United Kingdom, France and 
Canada have done it; even the United States  of America has done it; some of 
the more liberal democracies have also done it. Some have done it for their 
security forces; some countries have gone to the extent of doing it for those 
who are visually or physically chall enged; there are some countries which 
have also done it for the people, who on the day of election, are expected to 
be outside the country. Therefore, this is  also a facility, which has been given 
to them, and this system has started wo rking, as far as those countries are 
concerned. 
There are several other categories also, for instance, our missions 
abroad. But in those cases, the sy stem of sending them through the 
diplomatic bag, where the ballot paper itself can reach them in two or three 
days, is available to them. Therefore, after considering all these views, the 
Government has been of the view that this, perhaps, is an issue, which this 
House must take up for consideration. The Lok Sabha has approved this, and, 
therefore, the effective choi ce is between a difficulty which results in denial of 
right of franchise to a large number of our Army and Security personnel,  and 
alternatively giving them the option of voting also by a

must effectively live up to the expectations which some of our Forces have in

introduced. 
With these words, Sir, I commend to the hon. House that this Bill be 
taken up for consideration and acceptance by the House.

the basic tenets of our democracy, which is  secrecy of a ballot paper. Sir, the 
choice, here, is not between secrecy and openness. The choice here is, either 
allowing effectively no right to vote to our security personnel, or giving them an 
additional option of voluntarily relinqui shing their votes to a proxy of their 
choice, which is permitted under norms. This question of secrecy would arise 
if an alternative system of effective exer cise of vote were available, and we

parents, or, you will trust your adult children. And, if you don't trust anybody, 
then, please have some faith in the postal system. This is only an additional 
option that is being given to you. You ma y be a lucky one of the five per cent 
who may be able to vote through postal ballot. If you don't want to take a 
chance, you may take leave and caste your vote personally at the polling 
booth. These are all additional options t hat are available to you. There are, 
certainly, problems that you are created. But let me just mention - a number of 
Members would appreciate - that secrec y, in an election, is important. But 
secrecy does not get prim acy over the very 'right to vote' itself. When a 
number of us vote in a Legislative House, we vote by an open ballot. A 
number of Members have started thinking - that is one of the issues that this 
House may discuss in the near future - on the right to an open ballot in a 
Rajya Sabha election. I am conscious of the fact that there are two views on 
the matter. But that is also an issue th at is pending before this hon. House.

judgement of the Supreme Court which arose in the

came later in 1991, 1994 and 1999, for protecting the former Prime Ministers

arrangements also exist for the safety and security of VIPs and other

avoid any untoward incident involving any  VIP or a Minister or an important

a sense of security to the whole nation and specially taking care of the 
important leaders of this country. There is no doubt about it.
